class.name: PlantGenerator
class.brief_description: Generates small meadow plants (rosettes, clover, ferns, sedges, wildflowers) as meshes.
class.description: Builds a plant mesh from a [member preset] and a [member seed], after Prusinkiewicz et al., "The use of positional information in the modeling of plants" (2001): leaves, petals and florets are placed along their axes by phyllotaxis (the golden angle, Vogel's spiral for flower heads, whorls), their size, angle and bend are functions of their position, and leaves, petals and stems are swept along a turtle path. Each seed gives another plant of the same kind. The mesh has one surface per part (leaf, stem, petal, centre) with double-sided materials and back lighting, so light through leaves looks the same in raster and under path tracing. UV2.x holds a wind weight (0 at the root, 1 at the tips) and the vertex colour an occlusion guess. With [member lods], distance LODs are generated as the scene importer does. Use the meshes as [member PlantSpecies.meshes] in a [VegetationField3D]: [codeblock] var gen = PlantGenerator.new() gen.preset = PlantGenerator.PRESET_DAISY gen.apply_preset_colors() species.meshes = gen.generate_variants(3) [/codeblock]

method.name: get_bloom_shares
method.description: The shares of a preset's flowering stems on the day of [param season] ([member season]): [code]x[/code] none (leaves only), [code]y[/code] in flower, [code]z[/code] in seed. Use it to tell when a species' look has moved enough to generate its meshes again. Presets without a flowering window, and a season without [code]forcing[/code], give [code]Vector3(0, 1, 0)[/code].

method.name: get_drought_cure
method.description: The dead-tissue share summer drought gives a preset's leaves and stems on [param season] (its [code]soil_moisture[/code] and [code]temperature[/code]), the same soil-water ramp as [method GrassField3D.season_greenness]: open-ground grasses cure to straw, shallow-rooted forbs brown, deep-rooted forbs only yellow. [code]0[/code] for the evergreen shrubs, plants of wet ground, shade and the coast, in a frozen winter, and for a season without [code]soil_moisture[/code]. [method generate] applies it per plant.

method.name: get_pollen_amount
method.description: How much pollen a brushed plant of [param preset] sheds at full flower, relative (reedmace 1, meadow grasses 0.9, sedges 0.4); [code]0[/code] for insect-pollinated plants. The [code]make_*[/code] sets put it on their species as the meta [code]pollen[/code], with the preset as [code]plant_preset[/code], for [VegetationPollen3D].

method.name: get_pollen_release
method.description: The share of a wind-pollinated preset's plants shedding pollen on the day of [param season]: its flowering share ([method get_bloom_shares]) where its look has a flowering window, else its anthesis months by day of year (grasses late May to July, nettle and docks June to September). [code]0[/code] for insect-pollinated presets.

method.name: get_presence
method.description: The share of a preset's plants above ground on the day of [param season]: wood anemone, a spring plant, comes up in late winter and dies down by early summer; spider webs from spring (sheets) or late July (orbs) to late autumn, most in autumn; the mushrooms fruit from late summer to the first frost, more after rain (soil moisture) and most in autumn; every other preset is 1. [method make_floor] scales its densities by it.

method.name: is_parallel_sets
method.description: Whether [method make_sets] runs its calls on the worker threads ([method set_parallel_sets]).

method.name: make_dew_webs
method.description: Spider webs in open grassland as [PlantSpecies]: [constant PRESET_SHEET_WEB] over the sward and [constant PRESET_ORB_WEB] a few metres apart, in their season ([method get_presence]). The silk is drawn by the plant shader and shows only where dew or hoarfrost beads it ([WeatherMap3D] surface wetness and frost); a [code]"dew"[/code] key (0 to 1) in [param season] sets the dew instead, for scenes without a weather map.

method.name: make_hay_bale
method.description: A round hay bale ([constant PRESET_HAY_BALE]) for the seed: 4 x 4, 4 x 5 or 5 x 5 ft, lying on its side with the axis along +X.

method.name: make_bank_roots
method.description: Roots on bare scarps as two [PlantSpecies]: [constant PRESET_BANK_ROOTS] on any earthen face where the drawn ground drops 0.4 m or more past a steep edge ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_BANK_EDGE]), off rock, and [constant PRESET_BANK_ROOTS_WOODY] within 4 m of the canopy's edge ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_FOREST_EDGE]). Each variant is grown on its own face angle, 50 to 88 degrees (mesh meta [code]bank_face_slope[/code], radians); the field measures the face below each edge and takes the variant nearest it.

method.name: make_bank_turf
method.description: Turf overhangs as one [PlantSpecies] of [constant PRESET_TURF_LIP]: sod lips along the top edge of cut banks and scarps where the drawn ground drops 0.35 m or more past a steep edge ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_BANK_EDGE]; the field stands each on the edge, mesh +X over the drop), on grassy ground under 35 degrees.

method.name: make_flowering_grasses
method.description: Flowering meadow grasses for a sward: Yorkshire fog ([constant PRESET_YORKSHIRE_FOG]) in loose drifts through open grassland, and over it the waist-high heads of the tall meadow in their own drifts: false oat-grass ([constant PRESET_FALSE_OAT_GRASS]), and meadow foxtail ([constant PRESET_MEADOW_FOXTAIL]) and tufted hair-grass ([constant PRESET_TUFTED_HAIR_GRASS]) on the damper ground (RULE_WETNESS), and the tall flowers in their own drifts: ox-eye daisy ([constant PRESET_OX_EYE_DAISY]), meadow cranesbill ([constant PRESET_MEADOW_CRANESBILL]) and red campion ([constant PRESET_RED_CAMPION], also under part shade); heads by the [param season] (as [member season]): grasses none before heading, tinted in flower, straw in seed; flowers open by their own warmth. The species' far colour takes the heads' tint while they stand (none outside the season). Species carry the meta [code]flowering_grass[/code]. Place them ahead of a field's own tall grass so the drifts claim their room.

method.name: make_flood_wrack
method.description: A flood's leavings as [PlantSpecies] of [constant PRESET_FLOOD_WRACK]: the main strand line within 8 cm under the last flood's crest and thinner, sparser lines 0.35 to 0.9 m lower where the falling water left them ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_HIGH_WATER] from [method WorldWater.high_water_at]), laid along the contour ([member PlantSpecies.follow_flow]), for a year after the flood ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_FLOOD_AGE]). A [code]"flood_age"[/code] key (years) in [param season] ages the meshes. Put them ahead of the ground cover in [member Biome.species]: later species keep clear of earlier ones' footprints, and wrack lies over the sward.

method.name: make_fairy_rings
method.description: The mushrooms of meadow fairy rings as [PlantSpecies]: [constant PRESET_FAIRY_RING_MUSHROOM] along the rings' line ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_FAIRY_RING] -0.25 to 0.1 m), on the same world rings [member GrassField3D.fairy_rings] draws in the grass, out of deep shade, in their season ([method get_presence]).

method.name: make_floor
method.description: Returns the forest floor for a stand type as [PlantSpecies], bigger plants first: gap and edge plants in the half-light, shade herbs, mosses, twigs and litter on the closed floor. Each is placed by [constant PlantSpecies.RULE_SHADE] from the placed canopy and, where the stand matters, by [constant PlantSpecies.RULE_CONIFER] (leaf litter under broadleaves, needle litter and bilberry under conifers), so a mixed stand sorts its own floor. Append them to a [Biome] after its trees. The stands match the tree generator's stand types. Each species has the meta [code]floor[/code] set to [code]true[/code]. Brambles and bracken draw impostors past [param impostor_range] metres ([method add_impostors]); 0 keeps their meshes at every distance. The leaf litter is the stand's own fallen leaves ([method stand_litter_leaves]); [param season] is a season state as [code]WeatherMap3D.get_season()[/code] returns it, for the fallen colours, the share of fresh leaves and the flowering ([member season]). Broadleaf floors end with [constant PRESET_LEAF_BANK], leaf drifts where the wind gathers the litter ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_LITTER_DRIFT]); the leaf litter itself thins on crests and fills hollows by the same drift.

method.name: make_banks
method.description: Returns the waterside plants for a stream, a lake or a waterfall's spray zone as [PlantSpecies], placed by their distance to the water ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_WATER_DISTANCE]) in clonal patches: marsh marigold at the water's edge, butterbur colonies on stream banks, meadowsweet in the tall-herb band behind, and in spray ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_SPRAY]) thallose liverworts on the wet ground. The plants of the stones in the water are in [method make_stones] with [constant STONES_RIVER]. They do not colour the far ground. Each species has the meta [code]banks[/code] set to [code]true[/code]. [param season] is a season state as [code]WeatherMap3D.get_season()[/code] returns it, for flowering and the leaves' year.

method.name: make_alpine
method.description: Returns the plants of an alpine zone above the treeline as [PlantSpecies]. They grow above the treeline, where the growing season averages under 6.4 C ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_SEASON_TEMPERATURE], faded over 0.8 C; Paulsen and Körner 2014), so the map needs a climate. That follows the map's own treeline: low on an oceanic mountain with mild winters and cool summers, high on a continental one. Fellfield reaches 1 C of season lower, as wind-blasted ridges hold alpine heath below the treeline. The stands sort by snow lie and ground: fellfield cushions on convex ridges blown free of snow ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_CURVATURE]), the sedge sward on slopes with soil ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_SOIL_DEPTH]), dwarf willow and moss in concave, shaded snowbeds ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_SUNLIGHT]), and the scree set on talus ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_TALUS]). They do not colour the far ground. Each species has the meta [code]alpine[/code] set to [code]true[/code]. [param season] is a season state as [code]WeatherMap3D.get_season()[/code] returns it, for flowering and seed heads.

method.name: make_bog
method.description: Returns the plants of a bog as [PlantSpecies]: sphagnum hummocks and lawns, cotton grass, bog asphodel and sundew, with heather on the hummocks of a blanket bog. They keep to wet, nearly level ground ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_WETNESS], [constant PlantSpecies.RULE_SLOPE]) and share one patch noise per stand, the hummock species in its patches and the hollow species outside them ([member PlantSpecies.patch_invert]), so hummocks and hollows sort themselves. They do not colour the far ground. Each species has the meta [code]bog[/code] set to [code]true[/code]. [param season] is a season state as [code]WeatherMap3D.get_season()[/code] returns it, for flowering, the cotton and the autumn colours.

method.name: make_dry_tussocks
method.description: Perennial bunchgrass tussocks for summer-dry country, as geometry over the ground's cured cover: esparto ([constant PRESET_ESPARTO]) in the semi-arid steppe (RULE_PRECIPITATION 150 to 470 mm) and thatching grass ([constant PRESET_THATCHING_GRASS]) on the wetter dry slopes (320 to 850 mm), both under 1000 mm where the terrain cures its cover. They keep off rock, shade and the climate's bare patches, and cure by the [param season] as [method get_drought_cure] says. Species carry the meta [code]dry_tussock[/code].

method.name: make_dunes
method.description: Returns the plants of a sand dune zone as [PlantSpecies], placed by distance to the water ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_WATER_DISTANCE]) on slopes under dry sand's angle of repose: lyme grass and a little marram on the embryo dunes of the strandline, marram tussocks with lyme grass and sea holly on the mobile foredunes, thinning marram with a dry sward and moss on the fixed dunes behind. Grasses grow in clonal patches. Put the [VegetationField3D] in [code]GroundSurface3D.wind_shelters[/code] and the plants shelter the sand and trap it ([method VegetationField3D.sample_lateral_cover]). They do not colour the far ground. Each species has the meta [code]dunes[/code] set to [code]true[/code]. [param season] is a season state as [code]WeatherMap3D.get_season()[/code] returns it, for flowering.

method.name: make_heath
method.description: Returns the dwarf shrubs of an Atlantic heath zone as [PlantSpecies] (Gimingham 1972; Rodwell 1991). Heath is oceanic and open: over about 700 mm of rain a year ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_PRECIPITATION]), January means over about -4 C ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_JANUARY_TEMPERATURE]), out of the shade of crowns ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_SHADE] under 0.3), off bare rock, and below the alpine belt (growing season over 6.4 C, [constant PlantSpecies.RULE_SEASON_TEMPERATURE], where [method make_alpine] takes over). Dry heath (heather in patches of different ages, bell heather on the sunniest slopes, crowberry on the shaded ones, wiry grasses) keeps to free-draining ground ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_WETNESS] under 7.5); wet heath (cross-leaved heath, heather, cottongrass, sphagnum) to where water gathers, short of the bog (7 to 10); maritime heath (wind-pruned heather and bell heather, thrift, crowberry) to cliff tops open to the sea ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_COAST_EXPOSURE] over 0.4, 6 to 150 m above it, needing a geology source with a sea). They do not colour the far ground. Each species has the meta [code]heath[/code] set to [code]true[/code]. [param season] is a season state as [code]WeatherMap3D.get_season()[/code] returns it, for flowering and berries. With [param shrubs], TreeGenerator's gorse (mature and young, in clumps) and broom lead the dry set and wind-clipped gorse cushions the maritime one, two variants each ([method make_woody_shrub]); they are heavy meshes, so tests can leave them out.

method.name: make_saltmarsh
method.description: Returns the plants of a salt marsh zone or a shingle backshore as [PlantSpecies], zoned by height above the sea ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_TIDE_HEIGHT], metres for a mesotidal coast; Adam 1990, Rodwell 2000): glasswort and cord-grass on the pioneer mud (0 to 0.7 m), sea purslane, sea aster and sea lavender in a saltmarsh-grass sward on the low to mid marsh (0.5 to 1.3 m), thrift, sea lavender and sea rush in a fescue sward on the high marsh (1.1 to 1.9 m). The marsh keeps to sheltered coasts ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_COAST_EXPOSURE] under 0.3) on ground under 3 degrees, beach or not, since wave energy decides where mud settles. Shingle plants (sea kale, sea campion, yellow horned-poppy and thrift) grow on the beach's backshore ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_BEACH]) above the highest tides (1.8 to 4 m). The sets need a [member TerrainDataMap3D.geology_source] with a sea, and are not placed without one. Glasswort reddens from late August. They do not colour the far ground. Each species has the meta [code]saltmarsh[/code] set to [code]true[/code]. [param season] is a season state as [code]WeatherMap3D.get_season()[/code] returns it, for flowering and colour.

method.name: make_scrub
method.description: Returns the low aromatic shrubs of a Mediterranean scrub zone as [PlantSpecies] (Blondel et al. 2010; Flora iberica). Scrub is summer-dry and mild in winter: January means over about 3 C ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_JANUARY_TEMPERATURE]), 250 to 1,100 mm of rain a year ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_PRECIPITATION]), aridity 0.2 to 0.75 ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_ARIDITY]), out of the shade of crowns and off wet ground. Garrigue (open rosemary, thyme cushions and sage-leaved rockrose with bare stony ground between, and dry grass) keeps to thin soil ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_SOIL_DEPTH] under 0.45 m) and rock; maquis (closed sage-leaved rockrose and French lavender, a little rosemary) to deeper soil (over 0.35 m), under the tall shrubs added with [method apply_scrub_rules]. Thyme and lavender take the sunniest ground. Each species has the meta [code]scrub[/code] set to its stand. [param season] is a season state as [code]WeatherMap3D.get_season()[/code] returns it, for flowering and the rockrose's summer drought. With [param shrubs], TreeGenerator's lentisk, kermes oak, gum rockrose and dwarf fan palm lead the maquis, and kermes oak cushions, young fan palms and young gum rockrose the garrigue (the palm only where January averages 7 C or more) ([method make_woody_shrub]).

method.name: make_sets
method.description: Makes several species sets at once on the worker threads and returns their results in the calls' order, the same, resource for resource, as making them one after another. Each call is [code][method, args][/code], [code]method[/code] one of the static [code]make_*[/code] methods and [code]args[/code] its arguments as an [Array] (the ones left out take their defaults), or [code]["variants", preset, count][/code] for [method generate_variants] of a generator with that preset and its preset colours. The calls run on all workers but one (the main thread's rendering work needs one free); the slowest calls are best listed first. Call it from the main thread; [method set_parallel_sets] turns the threads off. [codeblock] var sets := PlantGenerator.make_sets([["make_heath", [PlantGenerator.HEATH_DRY, 3, true, season]], ["make_floor", [PlantGenerator.FLOOR_BEECH]], ["variants", PlantGenerator.PRESET_DAISY, 3]]) [/codeblock]

method.name: make_stones
method.description: Returns the plants between stones for scree, river gravel or shingle as [PlantSpecies]. The crevice plants keep to the gaps between the field's obstacles ([member PlantSpecies.stone_gap] 1), so they grow only where a [VegetationField3D] has stones in [member VegetationField3D.obstacles]; on river gravel moss, sedges and rushes gather at the stones' feet ([member PlantSpecies.rock_foot]), and on scree and river stones moss cushions grow on the stones' tops ([member PlantSpecies.stone_top], from [member VegetationField3D.stone_tops]): green ones on the low, shaded, north-tilted tops, smaller yellow-olive ones on the high, sunlit tops ([member PlantSpecies.stone_top_damp]). River stones sort by their tops' height over the water ([member PlantSpecies.stone_top_water]): aquatic moss trailing downstream on those under and just over the surface, liverworts on damp tops in the splash band, land mosses above the flood line. They do not colour the far ground. Each species has the meta [code]stones[/code] set to [code]true[/code]. [param season] is a season state as [code]WeatherMap3D.get_season()[/code] returns it, for flowering and the ferns' year.

method.name: set_parallel_sets
method.description: Whether [method make_sets] runs its calls on the worker threads (on by default) or one after another.

method.name: stand_litter_leaves
method.description: The leaves a stand drops, for [member litter_leaves]: one [Dictionary] per broadleaf species with its share of the litter ([code]share[/code]), its leaf form as the tree generator's [code]get_leaf_form()[/code] gives it ([code]kind[/code], [code]count[/code], [code]depth[/code], [code]width[/code], [code]size[/code]), its fallen colour ([code]color[/code]) and the share of fresh leaves among the older litter ([code]fresh[/code]). Forms and, with [param season], colours come from the tree generator when that class is present.

method.name: add_impostors
method.description: Gives a [PlantSpecies] impostors of its meshes ([method make_impostor]): its meshes move to [member PlantSpecies.near_meshes] and are drawn up to [param range] metres, the impostors beyond, with a dithered crossfade. Raster only: under path tracing [VegetationField3D] draws the meshes at every distance, so path tracing keeps the plants' depth and shadows. The species must not have near meshes yet.

method.name: apply_preset_colors
method.description: Sets the colours to the [member preset]'s natural ones.

method.name: apply_scrub_rules
method.description: Gives [param species] the climate and soil rules of a Mediterranean scrub stand, as [method make_scrub] does for its own plants, and sets its meta [code]scrub[/code] to the stand. Use it to place other scrub shrubs, such as a [code]TreeGenerator[/code] shrub species (gum rockrose, kermes oak, lentisk, dwarf fan palm), in the same garrigue or maquis.

method.name: generate
method.description: Builds the plant for the current [member preset] and [member seed].

method.name: generate_variants
method.description: Builds [param count] plants with seeds [member seed], [member seed] + 1, and so on.

method.name: make_climber_leaves
method.description: Returns [param variants] single-leaf [ArrayMesh]es of a climber ([constant CLIMBER_IVY], [constant CLIMBER_IVY_ADULT], [constant CLIMBER_CLEMATIS] or [constant CLIMBER_HONEYSUCKLE]; [constant PRESET_IVY] reads as ivy), for vines grown by other generators. Each leaf lies in the local XZ plane with its base at the origin, points +Z and is 1 m long; scale it per instance. Each carries the plant material, so it sways, wears, wets and takes snow and light like the ground plants.

method.name: make_impostor
method.description: Bakes an octahedral impostor of a plant (Brucks, 2018): the plant seen from [param frames] by [param frames] directions over the upper hemisphere, each [param frame_size] texels square and fitted to the plant, into an albedo and coverage atlas and a normal, depth and back light atlas. Returns a quad whose shader turns it to the view, blends the three nearest views, and moves each pixel to the plant's surface by the baked depth, so it meets the ground and casts and receives shadows like the mesh. Wind, wetness, snow and [VegetationField3D]'s far thinning work as on the plant shader. The quad has the meta [code]impostor_of[/code] set to [param mesh]. About 2.8 MB of textures with the defaults; baking runs on all cores.

method.name: get_burn_recovery
method.description: Returns the years a preset takes to full cover after a fire ([member PlantSpecies.burn_recovery]): grasses and sedges 0.7 (they resprout from their crowns within weeks), bracken, nettle and bramble 1.2, most herbs 1.5, litter 3, woodland herbs and ferns 4, bilberry 4, Mediterranean scrub 5, heaths 8, mosses 10, alpine cushions 15, soil crust 30. 0 for water plants and the burn presets, which [constant PlantSpecies.RULE_BURN_AGE] places instead.

method.name: get_trample_resistance
method.description: Returns the walkers a year that halve a preset's cover on a worn path, from trampling studies (Cole 1995). Plantain 1000, grasses 300, heaths and scrub 40, ferns 30; 0 for presets that are not ground plants.

method.name: make_avalanche_track
method.description: The ground layer of avalanche tracks as [PlantSpecies], placed only where [WorldStand] marks [constant DISTURBANCE_AVALANCHE_KIND] and by the years since the avalanche ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_STAND_AGE]): torn turf, broken twigs and shed needles in the first years, then fireweed, lady fern, raspberry, a broad-leaved tall forb and bilberry, on slopes up to 45 degrees. The bent shrubs are the trees'.

method.name: make_beaver
method.description: The plants of a beaver pond or of the meadow it leaves as [PlantSpecies] for a [Biome]. [constant BEAVER_POND] zones by water depth and distance from the shore: floating water lilies over 0.4 to 2 m, bulrush in the shallows, tussock sedge along the flooded margin, then soft rush, marsh marigold and meadowsweet up the shore. [constant BEAVER_MEADOW] grows on a drained pond bed, placed by [constant PlantSpecies.RULE_STAND_AGE] and [constant PlantSpecies.RULE_DISTURBANCE] on ground [method WorldStand.add_disturbance] marks with kind [constant DISTURBANCE_BEAVER_KIND] and an age of years since the pond drained: rush and small sedge on the mud for the first four years, then a dense sedge and tall-grass meadow with meadowsweet, marsh marigold and buttercup. Neither set takes shade over 0.4 to 0.6; the willow and alder that close an old meadow come from the trees.

method.name: make_rooting
method.description: What wild boar leave where they root, as [PlantSpecies] placed by [constant PlantSpecies.RULE_ROOTING] (years since the ground was rooted, from [code]WorldStand.rooting_age_at()[/code]; patches are [code]WorldStand.add_disturbance()[/code] discs of kind [code]DISTURBANCE_ROOTING[/code]): [constant PRESET_ROOTED_SOD] in three age bands (fresh, drying, slumped and greening) for the first year, then the first herbs on the turned soil, herb Robert, nettle and dock in [constant ROOTING_WOOD], mayweed, dock, thistle and plantain in [constant ROOTING_MEADOW]. List the set after the stand's own species. [method make_floor] gives its field layer rooting rules, so it is gone from fresh rooting and back over one to two years.

method.name: make_grazing
method.description: What grazing animals leave on their pasture, as [PlantSpecies]: dung ([constant PRESET_COW_PAT], [constant PRESET_HORSE_DUNG], [constant PRESET_DEER_PELLETS] at several [code]dung_age[/code]s, meta [code]dung_age[/code]) and the ungrazed roughs round it ([constant PRESET_DUNG_ROUGH]), with the weeds of enriched ground. Cattle reject the grass round their pats for months, so the lawn is dotted with rank tufts; horses dung in latrines and never graze them, so the paddock is a mosaic of lawns and roughs; deer leave pellet groups on their lawns ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_BROWSE]). All keep to the light (crown shade under 0.4, deer 0.9), slopes under 30 degrees and 2 m from water. Roughs and pats carry the meta [code]sward_mound[/code] (radius, m), so a [GrassField3D] whose [member GrassField3D.undergrowth_field] places them keeps its blades from under them. Place the set over the pasture (a mask or its own field); list it after the stand's species.

method.name: make_mounds
method.description: Anthills and molehills as [PlantSpecies]. [constant MOUNDS_MEADOW]: [constant PRESET_ANTHILL] in groups out of the shade (their crest east, so they are not turned at random), and [constant PRESET_MOLEHILL] fresh, crusted and grassing over, in lines and arcs (patch rings, a mole's runs). [constant MOUNDS_WOOD]: [constant PRESET_WOOD_ANT_NEST] at sunny gaps and edges of conifer and mixed stands ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_FOREST_EDGE] -2 to 40 m, crown shade 0.15 to 0.7) and a few molehills under broadleaves. None on waterlogged ground or steep slopes. Each species carries the meta [code]sward_mound[/code] (its radius at scale 1, metres): a [GrassField3D] whose [member GrassField3D.undergrowth_field] or [member GrassField3D.canopy_field] places them keeps its blades from under them.

method.name: make_burn
method.description: The plants of burnt ground as [PlantSpecies] for a [Biome], placed by [constant PlantSpecies.RULE_BURN_AGE] from [method WorldFire.burn_age_at]: each burn preset in bands of the years since the fire, its meshes built at that band's age (the season's [code]burn_age[/code]). Black stems with ash, then weathering silver-grey and falling; fire moss from three months to three years; fireweed as leafy shoots in the first year and flowering spikes from the second; tussocks green from the second week. Ground that never burnt takes none of them; the stand's other plants come back by their [member PlantSpecies.burn_recovery]. List these after the stand's own species in the [Biome]: a field places species in order, so the recovering plants claim their ground first and the burn plants fill what they leave.

method.name: make_desert
method.description: The plants of a desert sand sea ([member TerrainGenerator3D.sand_sea_rect]) as [PlantSpecies] for a [Biome], placed by [constant PlantSpecies.RULE_SAND_MOBILITY]: nothing on the moving crests and slip faces, drinn on the flanks and plinths, and on the stable interdune sand soil crust and the annuals, green after rain when [param season] has a soil moisture. With [param shrubs], [TreeGenerator]'s desert shrubs too: calligonum on the flanks' moving sand and young in the corridors, white broom and saltbush (the lowest, most stable flats) between the dunes.

method.name: make_woody_shrub
method.description: A [TreeGenerator] shrub ([enum TreeGenerator.Preset], [enum TreeGenerator.ShrubForm]) for a heath or scrub set: [method TreeGenerator.make_shrub_species] with at most two variants, the given density and clumps (patches); its climate and terrain rules are the caller's.

members.member: Colour of flower centres, heads and spikes.

How worn the leaves are, from [code]0.0[/code] (every leaf whole and green) to [code]1.0[/code]: uneven halves, round insect bites out of the margin with dried rims, dead tips on grass-like blades, and older, lower leaves yellowing and browning. Each leaf draws its wear from its own hash, so changing it does not change the plant's shape. The browning travels in the vertex colour's alpha.

Leaf and needle litter: how many times the card's own layers of leaves or needles lie on it. Above 1, more layers fall on top of the card's own (the same card from the same seed, so swapping one for the other only adds leaves), each a little higher, with broken twig ends among them: the dead-leaves model, where the top layer is what shows. [method make_floor] uses 2.5 for the litter's near meshes ([member PlantSpecies.near_meshes]) within 7 m of the camera.

For [constant PRESET_LEAF_LITTER]: the stand's fallen leaves ([method stand_litter_leaves]). Each card then carries about two layers of those leaves over its disc, picked by share and shaped by kind: simple, lobed with rounded lobes, palmate, pinnate (mostly loose leaflets, now and then a whole leaf) or digitate. Fresh leaves keep their fallen colour; older ones fade to a dull tan brown and curl. Empty: generic broadleaf litter. For [constant PRESET_SEEDLING]: each seedling is one of those trees, picked by share, with true leaves in its form at about two thirds of the adult size and its seed leaves above ground or not (none for oaks, strap-shaped for maples and ash, a broad fan pair for beech). Empty: a generic seedling.
If [code]true[/code], distance LODs are generated (meshoptimizer), so plants far from the camera draw a fraction of their triangles.
Colour of the petals and florets.

The season state as [code]WeatherMap3D.get_season()[/code] returns it; its [code]forcing[/code] (degree days above 5 C since 1 January) and [code]day_of_year[/code] set the flowering of the flowering presets. Each has a window in degree days from the British flowering records: wood anemone, violet and dandelion in early spring, wood sorrel and woodruff in spring, buttercup and sorrel in early summer, foxglove, clover, yarrow, knapweed, wild carrot, scabious and thistle through summer, heather late; daisy, clover, yarrow and herb Robert flower on and off through theirs. Before the window a plant is leaves only (tall flowers are rosettes); each stem then opens in its turn, goes to seed (dandelion clocks, thistledown, buttercup and anemone achenes, foxglove capsules filling the spike from the bottom, wild carrot nests) and, for the tall flowers, dies back to a brown stalk that stands through winter, a share of them into the next spring. Bracken and the woodland fern follow it too: croziers rise and unroll in spring, the fronds stand green through summer, yellow and die with the season's [code]senescence[/code] sum (or a hard frost), lodge under autumn storms and snow, and last year's dead fronds lie flat until the new ones have unrolled. Empty: every stem in flower or, for the tall meadow flowers, a quarter in seed; ferns full and green. A [code]browse[/code] entry (0 to 1) is deer browsing pressure: bramble keeps low spreading canes bitten back with blunt ends and short side shoots, raspberry canes are bitten at the leader and bush out below the bite, leaves are eaten whole or torn, and flowers and fruit grow scarce.
[constant PRESET_BANK_ROOTS] and [constant PRESET_BANK_ROOTS_WOODY]: the angle of the bank face the roots are grown on, in radians from level.
Seed of the random variation: each seed gives another plant of the same kind.
Size in pixels of the generated leaf and petal textures.

If [code]true[/code], leaves and petals get generated textures: veins grown by open venation (Runions et al. 2005) with widths by Murray's law, colour drift, dry margins and spots in the albedo, a normal map that sinks the veins, and a translucency map in the back light texture where the veins block light. Textures are baked once per preset, surface and seed variant and shared between meshes.

constants.constant: Dandelion: a rosette of toothed leaves at the golden angle, hollow stalks with a head of florets on Vogel's spiral.
Ribwort plantain: narrow upright leaves and long stalks with dark flower spikes.
White clover: petioles with three round leaflets, sometimes a globe flower head (florets on a Fibonacci sphere).
Fern: arching fronds with alternate lobed pinnae, longest mid-frond.
Sedge: a tuft of narrow V-section blades, sometimes stalks with brown spikelets.
Oxeye daisy: basal leaves, tall stems with a white ray flower and yellow disc.
Meadow buttercup: lobed basal leaves, branching stems with glossy yellow cup flowers.
Stinging nettle: a patch of erect stems with opposite, toothed, heart-shaped leaves and hanging flower strings.
Spear thistle: a rosette of deeply lobed spiny leaves and a branched stem with purple flower heads (first-year plants are rosettes only).
Yarrow: feathery, finely divided leaves and a flat-topped cluster of small white flower heads.
Broad-leaved dock: big wavy-edged basal leaves with red veins and a tall rust-brown seed stem.
Cock's-foot grass: a coarse tussock of broad blades with clustered, one-sided flower heads.
Timothy grass: a tuft of narrow blades with tall stems ending in a dense cylindrical spike.
Last year's dead grass: straw blades, bent, broken and lying flat.
Fallen leaves of several shapes and colours with a few twigs, lying on the ground.
A moss cushion: a low mound packed with upright shoots.
Bilberry: a dwarf shrub of branched green stems with small oval leaves and a few dark berries.
Bracken: a few tall fronds whose triangular, finely divided blades turn nearly flat, for woodland edges and clearings.
Bramble: arching red canes with leaves of three or five toothed leaflets and clusters of dark berries.
Foxglove: a rosette of soft toothed leaves and a tall spike of purple bells hanging to one side.
Common reed: a stand of tall culms with two ranks of drooping grey-green leaves and nodding purplish plumes, for shallow water and wet ground.
Bulrush or cattail: fans of long, twisting strap leaves and stiff stems carrying the dark brown cigar of female flowers with the male spike above, for shallow water.
Soft rush: a dense tussock of glossy leafless stems with pale brown flower clusters bursting from their sides, for wet pasture and marsh.
White water lily: round floating pads with a cleft to the stalk and a few white flowers on the surface. Its origin is the water surface (see [member PlantSpecies.floating]).

Needle litter: loose fallen needles lying across each other and a few cones, the relief over the needle carpet that [method VegetationField3D.get_floor_shader_code] draws on the ground under conifers.
Fallen twigs and small branches lying on the forest floor.
Wood sorrel: carpets of three folded heart-shaped leaflets on slender stalks, with a few white flowers; for shady woods.

Tree seedling: a thin zigzag woody stem with two-ranked oval, wavy-edged leaves, 8 to 75 cm tall; the youngest keep their broad seed leaves, older ones grow flat side sprays from the upper nodes (shade form).
Feather moss: wide, flat, yellow-green carpets as under spruce and pine.
Woodruff: a clonal patch of upright unbranched stems, 12 to 28 cm, with whorls of six to nine narrow leaves held level and small white four-petalled flowers at the top; beech woods.
Wood anemone: single stems with a whorl of three deeply three-lobed leaves two thirds up and one nodding white flower of six or seven tepals; the spring carpet of broadleaf woods.
Ivy as ground cover: creeping runners along the floor with glossy, dark, lobed leaves on stalks turned up to the light, overlapping into a low carpet; oak and ash woods.
Heather: a dwarf shrub of wiry branched woody stems clothed in short leafy shoots, some with spikes of pink-mauve bells; pine heath and acid open ground.
Common dog-violet: a rosette of long-stalked, rounded heart-shaped leaves with shallow rounded teeth, and nodding blue-violet flowers on arched stalks; half-shaded woods, hedge banks and grassland.

Herb Robert: a straggling herb with red stems, opposite leaves of three deeply lobed leaflets on long stalks, and small pink five-petalled flowers at the stem tips; woodland rides, gaps, edges and hedge bottoms.
Common knapweed ([i]Centaurea nigra[/i]): stiff branched stems to 0.75 m, heads a dark knob of bracts under a brush of purple florets; about a quarter in seed (knobs alone).
Field scabious ([i]Knautia arvensis[/i]): stems to 0.85 m with pairs of lobed leaves, flat lilac pincushion heads; about a quarter in seed (bristly balls).
Wild carrot ([i]Daucus carota[/i]): feathery leaves, a compound umbel of white florets with a dark centre floret; about a quarter in fruit, the umbel curled into a bird's nest.
Common sorrel ([i]Rumex acetosa[/i]): arrow-shaped leaves, a slender panicle of tiny whorled red flowers; about a quarter in rust-brown seed.
Fly agaric ([i]Amanita muscaria[/i]): 1 to 3 together, red cap with white warts, white gills, a ring and a bulb with volva rims; under birch and conifers.
Cep ([i]Boletus edulis[/i]): 1 or 2, a brown bun cap over a pale tube layer, a stout bulbous stalk; under oak, beech, spruce and pine.
Chanterelle ([i]Cantharellus cibarius[/i]): groups of 3 to 8, egg-yellow funnels with a wavy margin and ridges running down the stalk.
Brittlegill ([i]Russula[/i]): 1 or 2, a red cap over white gills and a white stalk, no ring.
Clouded agaric ([i]Clitocybe nebularis[/i]): 2 to 4 together, grey caps over decurrent cream gills; in litter, along fairy-ring arcs.
Honey fungus ([i]Armillaria[/i]): a tuft of 6 to 15 fused at the base, honey-brown caps with dark scales and a ring; beside stumps and logs.
Ivy (Hedera helix): palmate, shallow lobes, dark and glossy with pale veins.
Old man's beard (Clematis vitalba): pinnate, two pairs of ovate leaflets and one at the tip.
Honeysuckle (Lonicera periclymenum): ovate, short-stalked, dull green.

Ivy's adult shoots (Hedera helix), grown where an old stem reaches the light high on its support: ovate to rhombic, unlobed, tapering to a point, a little paler and glossier than [constant CLIMBER_IVY].
Parsley fern ([i]Cryptogramma crispa[/i]): a bright green tuft of finely cut fronds on acid scree, the fertile fronds taller and narrower; rusty after autumn.
Maidenhair spleenwort ([i]Asplenium trichomanes[/i]): a flat rosette of narrow fronds, small rounded pinnae in pairs along shiny black rachises; evergreen, old rachises bare. Rock cracks.
Biting stonecrop ([i]Sedum acre[/i]): a mat of short shoots packed with fat succulent leaves, yellow star flowers in June and July. Shingle, gravel, wall tops.
Mossy saxifrage ([i]Saxifraga hypnoides[/i]): a cushion of rosettes of narrow-lobed leaves, white five-petalled flowers on slender stalks from May to July. Upland ledges, scree, stream gravel.
Thrift ([i]Armeria maritima[/i]): a dense cushion of grass-like leaves with round pink heads on leafless stalks from April to September; papery brown heads after. Shingle, sea cliffs, mountain scree.

Marsh marigold ([i]Caltha palustris[/i]): a clump of long-stalked, kidney-shaped, glossy dark leaves and branched stems of golden cup flowers from March to May, then stars of green follicles. Stream and spring edges, marshes.

Meadowsweet ([i]Filipendula ulmaria[/i]): reddish stems 60 to 120 cm with pinnate leaves of toothed leaflets and frothy cream cymes from June to September; the dead stalks stand brown through winter. Stream banks, tall-herb fen.

Butterbur ([i]Petasites hybridus[/i]): stout lilac-pink flower spikes from March to May before the leaves, then round leaves 30 to 90 cm across on stalks up to a metre, dying back in autumn. Colonies on stream banks.

Aquatic moss of stream stones ([i]Platyhypnidium riparioides[/i], [i]Fontinalis[/i]): dark shoots 5 to 15 cm trailing along +X (downstream with [member PlantSpecies.follow_flow]), lying on the stone, still in the wind.
Thallose liverwort ([i]Conocephalum conicum[/i]): glossy green ribbons 1 to 2 cm wide forking in two, lying in overlapping mats on wet rock and in waterfall spray.

Bog moss ([i]Sphagnum[/i]): a low hummock 40 to 90 cm across of tightly packed shoots, their star-shaped heads (capitula) making the surface. Ochre-green by default; [method make_bog] sets red and green kinds.

Common cotton grass ([i]Eriophorum angustifolium[/i]): narrow channelled leaves 15 to 35 cm, stems 20 to 50 cm with two to six nodding spikelets that flower dark in April and May, then hang as soft white cotton balls from late May into August.
Bog asphodel ([i]Narthecium ossifragum[/i]): flat fans of curved iris-like leaves, spikes of yellow six-pointed stars in July and August, then deep orange capsules standing into winter.

Round-leaved sundew ([i]Drosera rotundifolia[/i]): a flat rosette 2 to 5 cm across of red, round leaves fringed with glandular hairs, each tipped with a glistening drop; small white flowers on a slender stem in July.

Marram ([i]Ammophila arenaria[/i]): dense, stiff tussocks of grey-green leaves 45 to 85 cm rolled tight into spines, a third of them dead and straw-coloured; pale, dense, spike-like panicles on stems to a metre in July and August, standing bleached through winter. The grass that builds foredunes by trapping blown sand.

Lyme grass ([i]Leymus arenarius[/i]): loose tufts of broad, flat, glaucous blue-grey leaves 30 to 60 cm, arching; stout spikes 15 to 28 cm, June to August. The pioneer of the embryo dunes on the strandline.

Sea holly ([i]Eryngium maritimum[/i]): a stiff, waxy, glaucous plant 20 to 40 cm of spiny, holly-like leaves, branching low, with round powder-blue flower heads in ruffs of spiny bracts from July to September.

Moss campion ([i]Silene acaulis[/i]): a hard, domed cushion 10 to 25 cm across of tightly packed rosettes of tiny linear leaves, the core dead and brown, studded with stalkless pink flowers in June and July.

Purple saxifrage ([i]Saxifraga oppositifolia[/i]): a prostrate mat of trailing shoots clothed in small, opposite, overlapping blue-green leaves, with stalkless purple-pink cup flowers just after the snow melts.

Mountain avens ([i]Dryas octopetala[/i]): a woody mat of forking prostrate shoots, dark green scalloped leaves with rolled margins crowded at the shoot ends, old leaves brown below; white eight-petalled flowers on short stems, then twisted silky seed plumes.
Curved sedge ([i]Carex curvula[/i]): dense tufts of fine, curved, grey-green leaves with withered tips, and short dark spikes. The sedge of the closed alpine sward on acid soil.
Dwarf willow ([i]Salix herbacea[/i]): a creeping carpet of buried stems with pairs of small round glossy leaves only 1 to 3 cm above the ground, and tiny reddish catkins. The plant of late snowbeds.
Alpine toadflax ([i]Linaria alpina[/i]): blue-grey, whorled, fleshy leaves on sprawling shoots that wander through moving scree, with violet snapdragon flowers with an orange palate.
Glasswort ([i]Salicornia europaea[/i] agg.): leafless candelabras of jointed, fleshy green segments 3 to 5 mm thick on bare marsh mud, turning red and purple in autumn.
Common cord-grass ([i]Spartina anglica[/i]): dense clonal clumps of stiff stems with flat, grey-green leaves spreading stiffly, and erect yellow-brown spikes that stand into winter.
Sea purslane ([i]Atriplex portulacoides[/i]): a low, sprawling shrublet densely clothed in opposite, silvery-grey, mealy leaves, lining the marsh creeks.
Sea aster ([i]Tripolium pannonicum[/i]): fleshy, narrow leaves and a flat-topped spray of pale lilac daisies with yellow discs (some rayless), late summer.
Common sea lavender ([i]Limonium vulgare[/i]): a rosette of leathery leaves and stiff, zigzag-branched stems with one-sided spikes of small lavender flowers whose papery calyces stand through winter.
Sea kale ([i]Crambe maritima[/i]): a low mound of huge, waxy, glaucous, crinkled leaves on shingle, with dense flat heads of white four-petalled flowers in June, then round pods.
Sea campion ([i]Silene uniflora[/i]): trailing mats of glaucous, fleshy leaves with white, notched-petalled flowers over swollen bladder calyces.
Yellow horned-poppy ([i]Glaucium flavum[/i]): grey-blue, crinkled, deeply lobed rosettes, branched stems with yellow poppies and long, curved seed pods.

Bell heather ([i]Erica cinerea[/i]): a dwarf shrub of wiry stems, dark glossy needle leaves in whorls of three with leafy tufts in their axils, and crimson-purple bells in short spikes, July to September. The driest, sunniest heath.
Cross-leaved heath ([i]Erica tetralix[/i]): a straggling dwarf shrub of the wet heath, grey-green downy leaves in whorls of four, and pale rose bells nodding in a tight cluster at each shoot tip.
Crowberry ([i]Empetrum nigrum[/i]): prostrate mats of trailing stems crowded with glossy, rolled needle leaves; black berries from August to October.

Rosemary ([i]Salvia rosmarinus[/i]): an erect, dense evergreen shrub of woody stems branching into leafy shoots crowded with dark, rolled, linear leaves; pale blue two-lipped flowers in the leaf axils from winter to spring.
French lavender ([i]Lavandula stoechas[/i]): a compact, grey-leaved bush of upright leafy shoots, each ending in a dense dark purple spike crowned by purple bracts, March to June.
Thyme ([i]Thymus[/i]): a low cushion of wiry woody stems and small grey-green leaves, with rounded heads of pale pink flowers, April to June.

Sage-leaved rockrose ([i]Cistus salviifolius[/i]): a low, sprawling shrub of wrinkled grey-green leaves and white, crumpled-silk flowers with yellow stamens on long stalks, April and May; woody capsules after. In the summer drought the leaves fold, grey and partly fall.
Corn poppy (Papaver rhoeas): an arable weed of field margins with scarlet flowers.
Cornflower (Centaurea cyanus): an arable weed of field margins with blue flower heads.
Scentless mayweed (Tripleurospermum inodorum): an arable weed with white daisy heads and finely cut leaves.
Cow parsley (Anthriscus sylvestris): the verge umbellifer with lacy white umbels in spring.
Pincushion moss (Leucobryum glaucum): tight, pale glaucous domed cushions 4 to 20 cm across on acid oak, beech and pine floors.
Ground ivy (Glechoma hederacea): creeping runners with pairs of kidney-shaped leaves on long stalks, a mat a few centimetres deep; short shoots with blue-violet flowers in spring.
Drinn (Stipagrostis pungens): the desert dune grass, dense tussocks of rigid rolled grey-green leaves, half dead straw, with open panicles of silvery plumed awns.
The rain-flush annuals of desert interdunes: small grasses and rosette herbs, green after rain (the season's soil moisture), dry straw otherwise.
Biological soil crust: a dark, knobbly, pinnacled skin of cyanobacteria, lichens and mosses on stable desert sand, flecked grey, green and orange.

Rosebay willowherb (fireweed) on burnt ground: clonal reddish stems 0.7 to 1.4 m with spiral lanceolate leaves and a raceme of magenta four-petalled flowers opening from the bottom up, long pods below that split to white fluff. Leafy shoots only in the first year after a burn (the season's [code]burn_age[/code]).

Fire mosses on burnt soil (Funaria hygrometrica with some Ceratodon purpureus): a low yellow-green carpet with a forest of orange setae and nodding capsules, green ripening to orange-brown, thickest about two years after the burn.

Burnt heather or scrub: black stem skeletons with ash on the tips, weathering silver-grey, breaking and falling over 2 to 5 years, green resprouts from the stem bases from the first season (the season's [code]burn_age[/code]).
A grass tussock after a fire: black stubble over a charred crown, a green flush from the second week, whole again by about a year (the season's [code]burn_age[/code]).

Reindeer lichen ([i]Cladonia rangiferina[/i], [i]C. stellaris[/i]): lumpy, cauliflower-like cushions 5 to 10 cm high of densely forked branches, pale ashy grey-green, the tips nodding one way. Carpets the dry boreal pine floor ([constant FLOOR_BOREAL_TAIGA]); crushed underfoot and some 40 years back after a fire.
Raspberry (Rubus idaeus): upright suckering canes of clearings and windthrows, pinnate leaves, red fruit on the second-year canes.

A deer lawn: a dense mat of fine bents and fescues grazed to 2 to 8 cm, most blade ends torn and drying pale over bright regrowth. [method PlantGenerator.make_floor] places it in the light where deer browsing is heavy ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_BROWSE]).

Boar rooting: 3 to 8 turf clods torn up and flung over, most grass side down with the pale roots up, the torn grass drying within weeks; by the season's [code]rooting_age[/code] (years) the clods slump and crumble and green shoots come up between them.

A yellow meadow ant hill: a grassed dome of fine soil about 0.7 m across, its crest east of centre (+x) and its long axis east-west, covered in fine fescue blades with thyme cushions on the south-east face and bare crumbs of fresh workings near the top (season [code]ant_workings[/code], 0 to 1).
A red wood ant nest: a thatch dome of needles and twig bits 1.2 m across on a mossy earth bank, with dark entrances mostly on its sunny side.
A molehill: a lumpy heap of loose soil about 0.4 m across with crumbs spilt round it; by the season's [code]mound_age[/code] (years) it crusts paler, slumps and grasses over.

A leaf drift: the stand's fallen leaves ([member litter_leaves]) heaped 8 to 18 cm deep over an ellipse 0.9 to 1.6 m long, over a dark, matted layer of half-rotted leaves. [method make_floor] places it under broadleaf litter where [constant PlantSpecies.RULE_LITTER_DRIFT] passes 1.35: hollows and the feet of trunks, logs and stones.
A cattle dung pat 20 to 30 cm across: by the season's [code]dung_age[/code] (years) glossy and olive when fresh, crusted grey-brown within weeks, broken into plates and grassed through over months.
A pile of horse droppings, 6 to 14 balls with straw fibres; by [code]dung_age[/code] paling, crumbling and spreading.
A deer pellet group, 30 to 90 pellets about a centimetre long in a heap and scattered; by [code]dung_age[/code] near black and glossy, then brown, dull and crumbling.
An ungrazed rough round old dung or in a horse latrine: rank, dark green grass 20 to 45 cm tall, shorter at its edge, with flowering culms and a few dead leaves.
The fairy ring champignon (Marasmius oreades): clusters of 3 to 8 small buff caps 2 to 5 cm across with a broad boss on slender pale stalks, fruiting from late May to November after rain.

A money spider's sheet web in the sward: mostly small flat sheets 5 to 10 cm across near the ground, some hammocks or domes up to 25 cm higher in the grass, with scaffold threads up to the blade tips.
A garden spider's orb web 15 to 30 cm across, hung between two dry stems with its frame and anchor threads; some leave one sector open.

A flood's strand line 1.2 to 2.6 m long along the high-water mark: silted straw, reed stem pieces, twigs and leaves over a matted mat, its landward edge sharp at the crest and its foot frayed; wet and dark at first, grey and dry within weeks, broken up over a year by the season's [code]"flood_age"[/code] (years).

The sod's lip over a cut bank or scarp, 0.7 to 1.5 m along the edge (+Z): a root-bound turf slab 10 to 20 cm thick standing out 12 to 35 cm over the drop (+X) from undercut soil, its cut face and underside dark topsoil, the sward's blades leaning out and hanging over the edge and roots trailing 10 to 45 cm from its underside.

The sward's fine roots bared on a cut bank or scarp face below its top edge (+X over the drop, +Z along it): a fibrous mat thinning with depth as grass roots do (Jackson et al. 1996), grown by space colonization on the face, lying on it, dipping under it and hanging free at the finest ends.
A tree's or shrub's roots bared on a cut bank: a few woody laterals coming out of the face, running along and down it and branching to fine ends.

A round hay bale lying on its side, the axis along +X: 4 x 4 to 5 x 5 ft (UF/IFAS EDIS AN326), hay strands wound round the body, the ends domed with the wound layers' spiral, twine in bands, settled a little flat.

Yorkshire fog (Holcus lanatus): a soft grey-green tuft with culms 30 to 90 cm, flowering May to August (Woodland Trust). Each culm heads by the season's forcing: a dense panicle of paired spikelet scales on hair-thin branches, opening in flower, closing and paling in seed, each culm its own tint from white-pink to purple-red.

False oat-grass (Arrhenatherum elatius), the tall hay meadow's grass: culms 60 to 150 cm with a loose, nodding, shining panicle 10 to 30 cm long of large awned spikelets (Stace), June to September. Headed for some weeks before the flowers open, straw in seed.
Meadow foxtail (Alopecurus pratensis): culms 30 to 90 cm with a soft cylindrical spike 3 to 13 cm long, grey-green, then purple with its anthers, April to June; the earliest meadow grass in head.

Tufted hair-grass (Deschampsia cespitosa): a dense dark tussock under culms 50 to 150 cm with a wide airy panicle of hair-thin branches, a silvery purple haze in flower, golden then straw in seed, standing through winter. Damp ground.
Ox-eye daisy (Leucanthemum vulgare): stems 20 to 70 cm, single heads 25 to 50 mm of white rays round a yellow disc, May to September; heads turn out and up from the plant.
Meadow cranesbill (Geranium pratense): stems 30 to 80 cm over deeply cut palmate leaves, pairs of violet-blue five-petalled saucers 25 to 40 mm, then beaked fruits, June to September.
Red campion (Silene dioica): stems 30 to 90 cm, loose forked clusters of rose-pink flowers 18 to 25 mm with five notched petals on dark reddish calyces, May to June. Tolerates part shade.

Esparto (Macrochloa tenacissima, Stipa tenacissima): a dense clump of wiry, rolled, grey-green leaves 30 to 60 cm arching out like a fountain, much of it standing dead straw; old clumps die in the middle into rings. Culms to about 1 m with a narrow panicle of pale spikelets and long plumed awns, March and April. Semi-arid steppe.

Thatching grass (Hyparrhenia hirta): a tuft of narrow grey-green leaves 20 to 45 cm under culms 40 to 95 cm, branched above, each branch with a reddish spathe and a pair of short racemes of white-hairy spikelets with dark bent awns; spring to autumn, curing straw. Dry Mediterranean slopes.
Number of presets.
Cattle pasture: pats fresh, crusted and old, an ungrazed rough round older pats, docks and nettles on rich spots.
Horse pasture: latrines (a quarter of the paddock in clumps, one patch layout for the set) with roughs, piles of droppings, nettles and thistles.
Deer lawns: pellet groups where [constant PlantSpecies.RULE_BROWSE] is 0.3 or more.
Number of grazing sets.
Beech wood: deep leaf litter, beech seedlings, woodruff, wood sorrel, wood anemone, few ferns.
Oak, lime and ash: a rich herb layer, bramble under the crowns, ivy carpets, wood anemone, ferns, bracken in gaps.
Montane spruce, fir and beech: wood sorrel, ferns and bilberry on mixed leaf and needle litter.
Subalpine larch and spruce: bilberry carpets, heather in the light, few herbs.
Pine heath: bilberry, heather and hair-grass under open crowns, bracken in gaps.
Riparian alder and willow: nettle, sedge and rush near water, ferns.
Hedgerow bottom: bramble, nettle, ivy, foxglove, fern.
Northern hardwoods (sugar maple, beech, birch): deep leaf litter, spring ephemerals, ferns, wood sorrel, many seedlings.
Eastern oak and hickory: oak litter with blueberry and huckleberry carpets, bracken in gaps, few herbs.
White pine and hemlock: deep needle duff, nearly bare; a little moss, wood sorrel and seedlings.

Cork and holm oak, stone pine (montado, dehesa): a continuous layer of dry annual grass, thinner in the crowns' shade; thistles and French lavender in the open, sage-leaved rockrose in loose patches, thyme; thin oak litter, needles under pine.

Boreal pine and spruce with birch in burn patches (the trees' boreal taiga stand): reindeer lichen carpets under open pine crowns, feather moss and bilberry under dense spruce, crowberry and heather in the open, wavy hair-grass and hair moss under the birch, birch litter there and needles under the conifers; fly agaric and brittlegills.
Number of floor stand types.
Acid upland scree and block litter: parsley fern, mossy saxifrage, maidenhair spleenwort, a little thrift, moss cushions on the blocks' tops.
River and stream gravels: mossy saxifrage, stonecrop, a little thrift, sedges and rushes at the stones' feet near water, moss.
Shingle above the strandline: thrift, stonecrop, a little dry grass.
Number of stone stand types.
A stream's banks: marsh marigold at the edge, butterbur on the banks, meadowsweet behind.
A lake's or pond's margin: marsh marigold and meadowsweet, no butterbur.
A waterfall's spray zone: liverworts and marsh marigold where the spray reaches.
Number of bank stand types.
Upland blanket bog: red sphagnum hummocks with heather, ochre sphagnum lawns, cotton grass, bog asphodel and sundew in the hollows.
Valley mire: green sphagnum in wet hollows, ochre on the hummocks, cotton grass throughout, bog asphodel, sundew and rush.
Number of bog stand types.
Embryo dunes on the strandline, 2 to 30 m from the water: lyme grass, a little marram, sea holly.
Mobile (yellow) foredunes, 5 to 120 m from the water: marram tussocks with bare sand between, lyme grass on the seaward foot, sea holly.
Fixed (grey) dunes, 80 to 400 m from the water: thinning marram, a dry sward, moss, a little sea holly.
Number of dune stand types.
Desert dune flanks and plinths: drinn tussocks, thinning towards the crests.
Desert interdune corridors: sparse drinn, biological soil crust on the stable sand, the rain-flush annuals.

Oases at desert springs ([constant PlantSpecies.RULE_SPRING]): trees' date palm oasis ([constant TreeGenerator.STAND_DATE_OASIS]) on the wet ground, and with [code]shrubs[/code] a ring of calligonum, white broom and saltbush where the water lies deeper. The interdune crust and annuals keep off its wettest ground.
Number of desert stands.
Burnt heather moor: charred stems, fire moss, fireweed, resprouting moor-grass.
Burnt grassland: resprouting tussocks, a little fire moss and fireweed in the gaps.
Burnt scrub: tall charred skeletons standing up to seven years, fireweed and resprouting grasses between.
Number of burn stands.
Rooting on a woodland floor.
Rooting in a meadow or at a wood's edge.
Number of rooting stands.
Old pasture: ant hills and molehills.
Woodland: wood ant nests and a few molehills.
Number of mound sets.
An active beaver pond and its shore.
A drained beaver pond bed, by years since draining.
Number of beaver stands.
The [WorldStand] disturbance kind of an avalanche track ([constant WorldStand.DISTURBANCE_AVALANCHE]), which [method make_avalanche_track] grows on.
The [WorldStand] disturbance kind of a drained beaver pond, which [constant BEAVER_MEADOW] grows on.
Fellfield on exposed ridges blown free of snow: moss campion cushions, purple saxifrage and mountain avens mats far apart on gravel, curved sedge in the lee.
Alpine grassland on slopes with soil: a closed sward of curved sedge, with mountain avens and moss campion in it.
Snowbeds in shaded hollows where snow lies late: dwarf willow carpets with dark mosses and a little sedge.
Moving scree: alpine toadflax wandering through it, purple saxifrage mats holding it, mountain avens over it.
Number of alpine stand types.
Pioneer marsh about mean high water neaps: glasswort scattered on bare mud, cord-grass in clonal clumps.
Low to mid marsh: sea purslane, sea aster and sea lavender in a saltmarsh-grass sward.
High marsh: thrift, sea lavender, sea rush and a little sea aster in a fine fescue sward.
Shingle backshore above the highest tides: sea kale, sea campion, yellow horned-poppy and thrift.
Number of salt marsh stand types.
Dry heath on free-draining ground: heather, bell heather, crowberry and wiry grasses.
Wet heath where water gathers, short of the bog: cross-leaved heath, heather, cottongrass and sphagnum.
Maritime heath on exposed cliff tops: heather and bell heather pruned low by salt wind, thrift and crowberry.
Number of heath stand types.
Garrigue on thin soil and rock: open rosemary, thyme and sage-leaved rockrose with bare ground between.
Maquis on deeper soil: closed sage-leaved rockrose and French lavender under the tall shrubs.
Number of scrub stand types.
